title: Legal-ism Mission Creep
gist: A serving Army JAG officer reviews Doyle Hodges's 'The Rise of US Military Legalism,' which argues U.S. commanders now justify force by parsing legal rules rather than exercising traditional professional judgment--illustrated by the 2019 Baghuz strike where a unit claiming self-defense on over 70% of its airstrikes killed about 70 people, mostly civilians, then cleared itself. The reviewer largely endorses the thesis while faulting its evidence base, which leans on a nearly two-decade-old Navy-only workload survey.

themes.theme: The Baghuz case as the paradigm

insights.claim: On March 18, 2019 a U.S. Air Force F-15E dropped a 500-pound bomb on a crowd of women and children near Baghuz, Syria, followed by two 2,000-pound bombs on the survivors, killing about 70 people, a majority of them civilians.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: The concrete case now anchoring critiques of U.S. targeting practice--relevant to how allies and courts assess American rules of engagement.
insights.locator: On the morning of March 18, 2019

insights.claim: By late 2018 more than 70 percent of the airstrikes called in by the special operations unit involved at Baghuz claimed self-defense under the law of armed conflict, which permitted bypassing the deliberative targeting review designed to limit civilian harm.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: When an exception carries 70% of cases, the review process it bypasses has effectively been nullified--a measurable indicator of process capture.
insights.quote: By late 2018, more than 70 percent of the airstrikes that unit called in claimed self-defense.
insights.locator: A special operations unit had called in the strike

insights.claim: After an Air Force lawyer watching the drone feed flagged Baghuz as a possible war crime and asked whether the self-defense claim had systematically circumvented the deliberate strike process, the unit that called in the strike conducted its own self-assessment and concluded the bombing was lawful with no further investigation or discipline warranted.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Self-adjudication by the acting unit is the accountability failure mode; institutional reform proposals will target exactly this.
insights.quote: intentionally and systematically circumvented the deliberate strike process
insights.locator: An Air Force lawyer who watched the drone feed

insights.claim: Doyle Hodges defines military legalism as 'the practice of privileging legal reasoning rather than traditional professional judgment in justifying military decisions regarding the use of force'--a deliberately narrow claim about officers' thought processes, not about the law growing more complex or rules multiplying.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: A precise analytical frame for reading defense decision-making; distinguishes a cultural shift from a regulatory-burden complaint.
insights.quote: the practice of privileging legal reasoning rather than traditional professional judgment in justifying military decisions regarding the use of force.
insights.locator: What Is Military Legalism?

insights.claim: The two hallmarks of military legalism are rule formalism--parsing rule text to reach results contrary to the rule's intent, what officers deride as 'barracks lawyer' work--and advocacy, where non-lawyer officers adopt the zealous-advocate posture instead of offering candid balanced professional advice.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Gives two observable diagnostics for spotting the phenomenon in any rule-bound organization, including compliance functions in finance.
insights.locator: Two hallmarks of military legalism

insights.claim: Hodges argues military legalism sets a commander's focus on the bare legal minimum rather than on expertise and ethics that could produce decisions both more effective and more ethical than the legal floor.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: The 'legal floor becomes the ceiling' dynamic generalizes to any regulated industry where compliance displaces judgment.
insights.locator: Hodges argues that military legalism contorts

insights.claim: Because the profession values both autonomy and obedience to civilian control, and policymaker constraints keep mounting, legalism becomes the path of least resistance--officers preserve operational latitude by reframing decisions as rule interpretation.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Explains why the behavior is structurally reproduced rather than a personnel failing, so it will not be fixed by leadership changes alone.
insights.locator: Yet as the number of constraints

insights.claim: Hodges borrows Samuel Huntington's 'managers of violence' framing and a principal-agent model of civil-military relations in which civilians set the political agenda and officers execute the corresponding military mission within a bounded sphere of autonomy.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: The theoretical scaffolding used in current civil-military debates; useful shorthand for assessing defense-institution behavior.
insights.locator: Borrowing Samuel Huntington’s characterization

insights.claim: Hodges traces the shift to post-WWII policymakers who feared nuclear escalation and imposed laws and regulations constraining commanders' latitude, with those constraints hardening in legal and normative form after My Lai and the 1974 Department of Defense Law of War Program.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Dates the origin of the constraint architecture--useful for judging whether current deregulation-of-force pressure is a reversal or a continuation.
insights.locator: Chapter 3 offers a theoretical account

insights.claim: The end of the Cold War made the United States a unipolar hegemon with capabilities beyond any adversary, which itself increased international and domestic scrutiny whenever Washington chose to deploy force.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Implies that as unipolarity erodes toward multipolar competition, the scrutiny premium--and thus legalism's pressure--may ease.
insights.locator: When the Cold War ended

insights.claim: The 2003 Iraq invasion intensified scrutiny specifically because the United States did not secure a UN Security Council resolution authorizing it and never found weapons of mass destruction.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Legitimacy shortfalls compound into lasting institutional constraints--a cost of unilateral action that shows up years later.
insights.locator: Hodges uses the 2003 invasion of Iraq

insights.claim: The reviewer adds that Nuremberg and successor tribunals established individual criminal responsibility for officers even when following superior orders, and the 1949 Geneva Conventions narrowed available military-necessity claims, so the postwar order did not merely invite scrutiny--it changed the personal penalty for getting war wrong.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Personal criminal liability, not institutional reputation, is the mechanism driving defensive legalism--the same logic that drives individual-liability-driven caution in corporate compliance.
insights.quote: the postwar order did not merely invite scrutiny; it changed the penalty for getting war wrong
insights.locator: But as Hodges’s own history shows

insights.claim: The U.S. variant of military legalism took root precisely because the United States bargained for the international order that made it possible, making the phenomenon a self-inflicted consequence of American order-building rather than an external imposition.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Reframes constraints on U.S. force as endogenous--relevant to debates over whether Washington should exit the institutions it built.
insights.locator: Whether or not military legalism is structurally inevitable

insights.claim: Insurgent and asymmetric forces have learned to exploit American commitments to civilian protection by fighting among civilians and provoking responses designed to generate outrage and challenge the legitimacy of U.S. action rather than to gain military advantage.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Legal and normative commitments are now an attack surface adversaries target directly--central to assessing modern conflict escalation risk.
insights.locator: He pays particular attention to adversary behavior

insights.claim: Domestic audiences judge legitimacy mainly by the rightness of the cause and are relatively forgiving of how service members fight, while international audiences scrutinize the manner of operations and apply stricter standards when the underlying cause is contested.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: A two-audience model for predicting political blowback from military operations--the split explains divergent domestic and allied reactions to the same strike.
insights.locator: Hodges argues that although the legitimacy

insights.claim: The military invariably becomes the institution most closely associated with any armed conflict even when it did not control the policy choices leading to it, so commanders use legal framing to preserve public esteem for the institution.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Reputation-shielding motive explains the behavior better than risk aversion--and means it persists across administrations.
insights.locator: Regardless of the audience

themes.theme: Institutional growth of the JAG function

insights.claim: Hodges measures military legalism through the institutional growth of each service's Judge Advocate General's Corps in absolute numbers and as a ratio to active-duty members, plus workload composition, rising operational-law publication by lawyers and line officers, and law's growing role in professional military education.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Gives the observable proxies for measuring legalization inside any institution--headcount ratios and workload mix.
insights.locator: He traces the institutional growth

insights.claim: The 1983 invasion of Grenada convinced the Army JAG Corps that dedicated operational law support was needed, leading to the 1988 founding of the Center for Law and Military Operations in Charlottesville, Virginia, to institutionalize legal lessons from operations.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
entities: Center for Law and Military Operations
insights.so_what: Pinpoints when legal advice became embedded in operations--the institutional origin of today's targeting-review architecture.
insights.locator: He traces this enhanced role in operational counseling

insights.claim: The reviewer's main methodological objection is that the book's quantitative core leans heavily on a 2007 Navy workload survey that is nearly two decades old, covered only Navy JAGs during the global war on terror, and offered no comparable Army or Air Force data to test the trend.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: The thesis is directionally accepted but empirically unproven--treat prevalence claims about military legalism as unquantified.
insights.quote: the quantitative core leans heavily on a 2007 Navy workload survey that is nearly two decades old
insights.locator: But even Hodges concedes

insights.claim: In the early-1980s Beirut intervention no lawyers deployed with the Marines on the ground, yet commanders justified restraint by formally parsing self-defense rules--suggestive evidence that legalism had been internalized, though Hodges concedes the restraint could equally reflect traditional honor and chivalry.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Shows the thesis's identification problem: restraint is observationally equivalent under both models.
insights.locator: The Beirut case is analytically important

insights.claim: In Iraq in 2003-04 the military had translated its professionalism into a series of legal 'if, then' statements that preserved operational autonomy while formally satisfying constraints, using the same self-defense exception invoked at Baghuz 15 years later.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the mechanism is stable and reproducible across two decades and multiple theaters, not incident-specific.
insights.quote: the military had translated its professionalism into a series of legal “if, then” statements that preserved operational autonomy even while formally satisfying those constraints.
insights.locator: The Iraq case figures as the better example

insights.claim: The Abu Ghraib abuses are characterized as a distorted reflection of legalistic interpretation, where policymakers and lawyers at the highest levels reviewed and approved enhanced interrogation techniques, creating a tacit top-down permission structure capable of shaping military culture broadly.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Top-down legal approval as a culture-setting mechanism--the clearest historical cost of the legal-floor approach.
insights.quote: a distorted reflection of a legalistic interpretation of the law that allowed the use of nudity, dogs, and stress positions (among other techniques)
insights.locator: He hearkens back to his experience

insights.claim: Hodges declines to condemn military legalism outright, conditioning the verdict on whether legal reasoning complements or supplants professional ethics, and cites the 2006 counterinsurgency field manual--drafted with human rights organizations, journalists, lawyers and academics alongside military experts--as the complementary case.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Identifies the design condition under which legal input improves rather than degrades decisions: inclusion at the drafting stage rather than as after-the-fact clearance.
insights.locator: In his final chapter

insights.claim: The failure modes Hodges fears are officers becoming rule-following technocrats more concerned with what rules allow than with doing what is right, or conversely exploiting rules for parochial ends while appearing compliant--both symptoms of degraded civil-military norms that rest on unwritten expectations rather than formal rules.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: Norm erosion in civil-military relations is a tail risk with no formal backstop--worth monitoring given the growing salience of domestic military deployment questions.
insights.quote: rule-following technocrats who are more concerned with what the rules allow than with doing what is right
insights.locator: Hodges’s larger concern

insights.claim: The reviewer, a serving lieutenant colonel who advised commanders on the use of force in Operation Iraqi Freedom, says the legalistic reflex extends well beyond the use of force and calls the Department of Defense Law of War Manual's 1,000-plus pages evidence that the mission creep of legal thinking was nearly foregone.
insights.speaker: Matthew Forst
insights.so_what: First-hand practitioner corroboration plus a hard measure of legal-corpus size--the trend is entrenched and unlikely to reverse.
insights.quote: The Department of Defense Law of War Manual is over 1,000 pages long
insights.locator: The mission creep of legal thinking
